title: Caching Fundamentals
summary: Why caching exists, where caches live across the stack, and what actually belongs in one — the vocabulary every other caching topic builds on.

slides.markdown:
A **cache** is a small, fast copy of data that lives closer to where it's used, so you don't pay the full cost of fetching it from the source every time. Think of it like keeping frequently-used spices on the counter instead of walking to the pantry each time you cook.

Caching shows up everywhere in a system — the browser, the CDN, the app server, in front of the database — and every layer trades a bit of staleness risk for a lot of speed. This topic covers the vocabulary: why caches exist, where they sit, and what deserves to be cached at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Why caching exists: the latency/cost gap it closes
slides.markdown:
Every data fetch has a cost: a disk read, a network hop, a database query, an expensive computation. A **cache** stores the result of that work somewhere faster and cheaper to reach — RAM instead of disk, a nearby server instead of one across the ocean — so the next request for the same thing skips the expensive path entirely.

Concretely: a database query might take 50ms; the same value read from an in-memory cache takes under 1ms. At 10,000 requests/second, that gap is the difference between a database falling over and a system that barely notices the load.

The takeaway: caching doesn't make data cheaper to produce — it makes *reproducing* an already-known answer nearly free.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: where caches sit — browser, CDN, app, DB
slides.markdown:
![Request path through four caching layers](assets/cache-layers.svg)

A single request can pass through four separate caches before it ever touches a disk: the **browser cache** (skips the network for static assets), the **CDN** (skips the trip to your origin server), the **application cache** (skips a database query, often Redis or an in-process cache), and a **database-level cache** (skips a disk read for a hot page or query plan).

Each layer only helps for its own kind of request — a browser cache does nothing for a database query, and vice versa — which is why a well-cached system usually has caching at more than one layer, not just one.

assets.alt: Request path through four caching layers

slides.sectionTitle: Cache hit, miss, and hit ratio as the metric that matters
slides.markdown:
A **cache hit** means the requested data was found in the cache; a **cache miss** means it wasn't, so the system falls through to the slower source (and usually stores the result for next time). The **hit ratio** — hits divided by total requests — is the single number that tells you whether a cache is earning its keep.

A product catalog page cache might run a 95% hit ratio because the same few thousand items get viewed constantly. A cache in front of highly unique, one-off queries might sit at 10% — barely worth the memory it uses.

When you're asked to design a cache in an interview, naming the *expected* hit ratio for your access pattern is what separates a real answer from "just add a cache."

An **in-process cache** (a hashmap living inside your application's own memory) and an **external cache** (a separate service like Redis or Memcached) solve the same problem at different scopes.

| | In-process cache | External cache (Redis/Memcached) |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Fastest — no network hop | Slightly slower — one network round trip |
| Shared across servers? | No — each instance has its own copy | Yes — every app server reads the same data |
| Survives a restart? | No — lost when the process restarts | Yes — lives independently of any app instance |
| Memory limit | Bounded by the app server's own RAM | Its own dedicated, scalable memory pool |

**How to decide:** use an in-process cache for small, per-instance data (like a parsed config) where a little duplication is fine; use an external cache the moment multiple servers need to see the same cached value.

slides.sectionTitle: What belongs in a cache vs what doesn't
slides.markdown:
Good cache candidates are **read-heavy, expensive-to-compute, and tolerant of slight staleness** — a user's profile, a rendered product page, a search result. Bad candidates are data that's **write-heavy, must always be exactly current, or accessed only once** — a bank balance mid-transaction, a one-time password, a report nobody re-reads.

The test isn't "is this data read often" alone — it's read-often *and* safe-to-be-slightly-stale. A view counter that's 5 seconds behind is fine; an inventory count that's 5 seconds behind can oversell the last item in stock.

When scoping what to cache, ask: how bad is it if this value is wrong for a few seconds? If the answer is "very," that's a signal to cache elsewhere or invalidate aggressively, not to skip caching design entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: caching data that changes faster than the cache is refreshed
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Caching always makes things faster and safer, so cache aggressively by default."

**Why it's wrong:** if the underlying data changes faster than the cache refreshes — a live stock price cached for 60 seconds, or an inventory count during a flash sale — the cache actively serves *wrong* answers, and it does so at high speed and high volume, which makes the problem worse, not better.

**Correct model:** before caching anything, match the cache's freshness window to how fast the real data actually changes. If a value changes every second, a 60-second cache isn't an optimization — it's a bug that looks fast.
